'''Egyptian Magic''' is an "all-purpose skin cream" founded in 1991, notable here less as a cosmetics brand than as a '''cultural thread''' the Library has researched directly: its founder, its bee-based formula, and its ancient-Egyptian framing sit precisely at the crossroads of the [[Zar]] tradition and the [[Punic Wax]] / wax-technology work. It appears in [[Media and Personalities]] among the adjacent threads, not the people.

== The product and its formula ==

Egyptian Magic is a simple salve built on honeybee and olive products: '''olive oil, beeswax, honey, royal jelly, propolis''' (and, per most listings, bee pollen) — fragrance-free and preservative-free, marketed as a single cream that serves as moisturizer, balm, and salve. The ingredient list is the first point of interest: it is, almost exactly, the materia of the ancient wax-and-resin cosmetic-medicinal tradition the Library documents under [[Punic Wax]] and the [[Egyptian Wax Headcones|wax head cone]] research — beeswax and bee products used as the base of a healing, anointing substance.

== The founder ==

The brand was founded by '''LordPharaoh ImHotepAmonRa''', born '''Westley Howard''', who — by his own account — received the formula from a mysterious mentor in the mid-1980s as a revival of ancient Egyptian healing, hand-blended the first jars in a small Washington, D.C. apartment, and grew the business entirely by word of mouth, at first literally trading jars for food at an organic market. He then changed his legal name to match the brand's pharaonic identity.

That figure — a man who takes a '''pharaonic name''', builds a product around an '''ancient-Egyptian bee-and-wax healing formula''', and transmits it as a kind of received secret — is the thread. It is the same shape the Library traces elsewhere: the anointing wax, the Egyptian healing frame, and the idea of a spiritual "technology" passed from teacher to student.

== Where it connects ==

In the [[Van Kush Family|Van Kush]] synthesis, Egyptian Magic is named in the same breath as the [[Zar]] tradition and [[Punic Wax]] as one of the "ancient spiritual technologies" — bee-wax medicine, spirit-healing, and anointing read as one continuous lineage of body-and-spirit craft rather than three unrelated curiosities. That is the Library's interpretive position, held as a position: we document the brand's own (promotional, unverified) origin story plainly, and then note where its materials and its mythos rhyme with the older traditions we study.
